question: You are a Senior Pharmacy Technologist in charge of the main medicines store. In your ABC inventory analysis, which strategy best suits Category A items?
options: Tight control with frequent counts, accurate stock cards and carefully set safety stock
Order in bulk once a year to get supplier discounts
Check them only once a year, because there are very few of these items
Keep very large safety stocks so a stock-out can never happen

explanations.correct_reason: Category A items are the few products (often 10-20% of lines) that make up most of the stock value (often 70-80%). They need the tightest control: frequent counts, exact stock card entries, regular demand checks, frequent small orders and lean safety stock. In practice: if your store holds expensive items like insulin pens or oncology injectables, count them weekly and reconcile with the stock card. One missing carton can cost more than a whole shelf of paracetamol.
incorrect_reasons: Annual bulk buying suits cheap Category C items like cotton wool. Example: buying a year of an expensive injectable at once ties up money and risks the whole lot expiring.
Few items does not mean unimportant. Example: your 20 costliest products may be 75% of stock value, so yearly checks let losses and expiry go unnoticed for months.
Large safety stocks of costly items waste money. Example: holding six months of a costly drug 'just in case' means it sits on the shelf and may expire. Watch demand closely and reorder often instead.

question: A Principal Pharmacy Technologist audits discharge medication supply records each week to confirm that every pack issued matches the pharmacist-approved prescription, and corrects any gaps found. Which function of the management cycle is this?

explanations.correct_reason: Controlling means checking actual work against the standard and correcting deviations. In practice: you pull 20 discharge records, find that 5 packs were issued without the label counselling note, then retrain the junior technologists and re-audit next week. That check-and-correct loop is control.
incorrect_reasons: Planning is deciding in advance what to do. Example: writing the discharge-supply procedure before it starts. The audit happens afterwards.
Organizing is arranging people and resources. Example: assigning a technologist to the discharge counter. An audit checks results rather than setting up structure.
Leading is motivating and guiding people. Example: encouraging the team before a busy week. An audit measures output, not morale.

question: Which option best describes the role of a Pharmacy Technologist under Good Pharmacy Practice (GPP), working alongside the pharmacist?
options: Making independent clinical decisions, such as changing a prescribed dose, without the pharmacist
Supporting the safe preparation, dispensing and supply of medicines under pharmacist supervision, managing stock and storage, and keeping professional skills up to date
Focusing only on sales targets and skipping routine stock checks
Marketing products, managing property and processing insurance claims only

explanations.correct_reason: GPP puts patient safety first. The technologist supports the pharmacist by preparing and dispensing medicines, labelling, storing and issuing stock correctly, keeping records, referring clinical questions to the pharmacist and continuing to learn. Senior technologists also supervise juniors and run stores. In practice: you pick and label an antibiotic correctly, the pharmacist does the final check and counselling, and you rotate stock by expiry.
incorrect_reasons: Dose changes and clinical judgement belong to the pharmacist and prescriber. Example: if a prescription dose looks unusual, you stop and refer it to the pharmacist instead of altering it.
Sales matter for survival but never replace safety. Example: skipping stock checks to serve more customers can lead to expired or wrong items being supplied.

Marketing, property and claims support a business but they are not the professional roles GPP sets for technologists. Example: processing a claim helps cash flow, but safe dispensing and storage protect patients.

question: During a storm the power fails and the vaccine fridge in the pharmacy store starts to warm. Which management practice would best have prepared the technologists running the store?
options: Setting SMART sales targets for the quarter
Contingency planning: backup power or cool boxes, a temperature alarm, a written cold-chain emergency procedure and an agreement to move stock to another site
Doing an ABC analysis of all stock

explanations.correct_reason: Contingency planning prepares for likely problems before they happen. In practice: when power fails at 2am, the alarm calls the technologist on duty, who moves vaccines into validated cool boxes with ice packs within minutes, records temperatures, and informs the pharmacist. Thousands of Pula worth of stock and patient safety are protected.
incorrect_reasons: SMART targets set goals but do not protect stock in an emergency. Example: a target of +10% sales does nothing when the fridge warms.
ABC analysis shows which items are most valuable but gives no action steps. Example: you know vaccines are Category A, but not where to move them tonight.
Appraisals review staff performance. Example: a good appraisal will not keep vaccines cold during an outage.

question: A junior Pharmacy Technologist receives opposite instructions about priorities from the Senior Pharmacy Technologist in charge of the store and from the Head of Pharmacy at the same time. Which management principle has been violated?

explanations.correct_reason: Unity of command means each employee takes orders from one superior for a given task. In practice: the senior technologist says 'finish the stock count first' while the Head of Pharmacy says 'issue the ward orders first'. The junior does not know whose order to follow, so one task is late or done wrongly. Solution: instructions should flow through the direct supervisor.
incorrect_reasons: Division of work is about specialising tasks. Example: one technologist dispenses while another manages the store. The problem here is two bosses, not how tasks are split.
Esprit de corps is team spirit. Example: celebrating team achievements together. Conflicting orders may hurt morale, but the principle breached is unity of command.
Remuneration is fair pay. Example: paying a technologist for overtime. Pay is not the issue here.

question: A Senior Pharmacy Technologist plans a quarterly review of the store SOPs and stock cards. Nothing is overdue, but the review matters for long-term quality. Where does it sit in the Eisenhower Matrix and what should be done?
options: Quadrant 1 (urgent and important): do it immediately
Quadrant 4 (neither urgent nor important): eliminate it

explanations.correct_reason: A task that matters but has no deadline is Quadrant 2, so schedule it. In practice: put 'quarterly SOP and stock card review' in the calendar as a fixed 2-hour slot. If skipped, an outdated procedure may cause a stock error or a failed inspection, and the task becomes a Quadrant 1 crisis.
incorrect_reasons: Quadrant 1 is for crises. Example: a product recall or a ward waiting for urgent medicine. A routine review is not a crisis.
Quadrant 3 is urgent but low value. Example: a non-essential phone call. SOP review is high value and should not be handed off carelessly.
Quadrant 4 is time-wasting. Example: scrolling social media at work. Dropping SOP reviews risks compliance and patient safety.

question: A Principal Pharmacy Technologist notices that the junior technologists work faster after she starts asking about their concerns and showing real interest in their wellbeing. Which theory does this best illustrate?

explanations.correct_reason: Elton Mayo's Hawthorne studies found that attention, recognition and good relationships raise productivity, sometimes more than pay or conditions. In practice: a senior who asks 'what slows you down?' and then fixes the awkward label printer often gets faster, happier work at little cost.
incorrect_reasons: Scientific Management focuses on standard methods and pay incentives. Example: timing each prescription and paying bonuses for speed, with little interest in feelings.
Weber's bureaucracy relies on strict rules and hierarchy. Example: staff must use a fixed form for every request regardless of personal concerns.
Fayol described management functions and principles such as unity of command. His focus was structure, not the social side of work.

question: The pharmacy buys an automated dispensing cabinet for P100,000. It saves P30,000 per year in staff time and wastage. What is the annual return on investment (ROI)?

explanations.correct_reason: ROI = annual gain / cost x 100 = 30,000 / 100,000 x 100 = 30% per year. In practice: you recover the cost in about 3.3 years (100,000 / 30,000). If the cabinet lasts 10 years, it pays back its cost about three times, so it is a worthwhile purchase. Senior technologists use such figures when motivating equipment purchases.
incorrect_reasons: 70% is 100% minus 30%, the part of cost not yet recovered after year one. It is not the return.
333% comes from dividing cost by savings (100,000 / 30,000 = 3.33), which is the payback period in years, not a percentage return.
3% is a decimal slip. 30,000 / 100,000 = 0.30, which is 30%.

question: Which of the following is a SMART goal for a hospital pharmacy dispensary led by a Senior Pharmacy Technologist?
options: Reduce the average outpatient prescription waiting time from 20 to 12 minutes within six months by adding a second labelling station
Be the best dispensary in the district
Try to reduce dispensing errors as much as possible soon

explanations.correct_reason: A SMART goal is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. This goal has a number (20 to 12 minutes), a deadline (six months) and an action (second labelling station). In practice: you record waiting times now, add the station, and check monthly. After six months you know clearly whether you succeeded.
incorrect_reasons: 'Improve customer service' is vague. Example: if waiting falls by one minute, did you succeed? Nobody can say.
'Best dispensary in the district' cannot be measured and has no deadline. Best by speed, safety or patient reviews?
'As much as possible soon' has no target or date. Example: a drop from 10 to 9 errors might count as success, and 'soon' could mean next year.

question: A Pharmacy Technologist packs insulin in cool boxes with temperature loggers and delivers it to the wards at 2-8°C. Which GxP standard governs this activity?

explanations.correct_reason: Good Distribution Practice covers storage and transport so medicine quality is kept until it reaches the patient: correct temperature, loggers, documented handovers and traceability. In practice: if the logger shows 12°C for three hours, the insulin is quarantined and the pharmacist is told. It is not issued until a quality decision is made.
incorrect_reasons: GMP covers making medicines. Example: controlling a factory line and batch records. Transport after manufacture is not GMP.
GLP covers laboratory safety studies. Example: recording animal toxicity results correctly. It has nothing to do with delivery of stock.
GCP covers clinical trials on people. Example: informed consent forms for trial participants. It does not govern routine ward delivery.

question: Which leadership style is most appropriate for a Principal Pharmacy Technologist supervising a highly experienced, self-motivated technologist who needs little supervision?

explanations.correct_reason: Laissez-faire (delegative) leadership gives skilled, self-driven staff freedom to decide how they work, with support when needed. In practice: a technologist with 10 years' experience runs the stock reorder system independently and only reports problems. This builds ownership and frees the senior for planning. It would be risky with a new, inexperienced technologist.
incorrect_reasons: Autocratic leadership means the leader decides everything. Example: telling an expert how to count each box. It suits emergencies or beginners and would demotivate a skilled person.
Paternalistic leadership means acting like a protective parent who decides what is best. Example: approving every small task. It limits a capable person's independence.
Bureaucratic leadership depends on strict rules. Example: requiring a signed form for every minor decision. It slows down an experienced person who can use judgement.

question: In a SWOT analysis for a hospital outpatient pharmacy, a new private pharmacy is planned to open right at the hospital gate. For the outpatient pharmacy, this is a:

explanations.correct_reason: Threats are outside factors you cannot control that could hurt you. A private pharmacy at the gate may take patients with shorter queues and longer hours. In practice: the outpatient pharmacy responds by cutting waiting time, improving stock availability and offering clear labelling and counselling support.
incorrect_reasons: A strength is an internal advantage. Example: well-trained technologists. A competitor's arrival is external and not an advantage.
A weakness is an internal limitation. Example: frequent stock-outs of common medicines. The competitor is outside your pharmacy.
An opportunity is a favourable external factor to use. Example: a new clinic opening that will send patients to you. A rival is the opposite.

question: Which statement best distinguishes leading from managing in a pharmacy department?
options: Leading plans, budgets and controls processes; managing inspires people towards a vision
Leading and managing are identical activities
Leading inspires and influences people towards a vision and change, while managing plans, organizes and controls processes to deliver stable results
Leading applies only to pharmacists, while managing applies only to technologists

explanations.correct_reason: Management keeps things running: plan, budget, organise, staff and control. Leadership sets direction and inspires people through change. In practice: a senior technologist who prepares the duty roster and checks stock is managing; the same person who convinces the team to start a new ward stock-checking system and keeps them motivated through the first weeks is leading. Good senior technologists do both.
incorrect_reasons: This swaps the roles. Building the roster and budget is management, while inspiring people is leadership.
They overlap but are not identical. A person can run a flawless roster without inspiring anyone, and a junior technologist can lead by mentoring a new colleague.
Neither depends on profession or rank. A junior technologist who mentors interns is leading, and a pharmacist who approves budgets is managing.

question: The store holds two batches of the same medicine: Batch A (received first, expires in 12 months) and Batch B (received later, expires in 4 months). Which rule should the technologist follow when issuing stock?
options: FEFO (First Expired, First Out): issue Batch B first
FIFO (First In, First Out): issue Batch A first
Issue the larger batch first to clear shelf space
Issue whichever batch has the lower unit cost first

explanations.correct_reason: FEFO issues stock closest to expiry first, whatever its arrival date. In practice: when new stock arrives, place shorter-dated packs at the front and record expiry on the stock card. Batch B (4 months) goes out before Batch A (12 months), so nothing expires on the shelf and patients always receive in-date medicines.
incorrect_reasons: FIFO uses arrival date only. Example: issuing Batch A first leaves Batch B to expire in 4 months, wasting money. FIFO works only when older stock also expires first.
Batch size does not affect expiry risk. Example: finishing the big batch first leaves the small short-dated batch to expire unused.
Cost is not a safe rule. Example: using the cheaper pack first ignores expiry and may leave expensive short-dated stock to expire.

question: After starting a chronic-medicine refill programme, a Senior Pharmacy Technologist checks pick-up records and pill counts at four weeks, compares them with the agreed adherence target, and adjusts reminders. Which management function does this represent?

explanations.correct_reason: Controlling means measuring results against goals and correcting course. In practice: at four weeks you find that 8 of 30 patients missed their refill, so you call them, shift reminder timing and refer clinical concerns to the pharmacist. This feedback loop is what makes the refill programme work.
incorrect_reasons: Planning happened earlier when the targets were set. Example: aiming for 90% on-time refills. The follow-up checks whether the plan worked.
Organizing arranges people and resources. Example: setting up a refill desk and appointment slots. The follow-up is evaluation, not setting up.
Leading is motivating and guiding people. Example: encouraging patients to keep going. The defining act here is measuring and correcting.
